claims.text: The starting MPEA is brittle at room temperature.
Conventionally cast material has equiaxed grains and randomly oriented grain boundaries.
A significant volume fraction of Heusler or Laves intermetallic phases acts as room-temperature crack-initiation sites.
Bridgman directional solidification at 3 mm/min through a water-cooled baffle produces grains elongated along the tensile loading direction.
Annealing at 900 °C for 50 h reduces the Heusler fraction from about 9% to 3% and retains smaller γ′ precipitates of about 200 nm rather than 400 nm.
The optimized anneal produces spherical or sharp-cornered γ′ precipitates.
Combining directional solidification with optimized low-temperature annealing simultaneously increases yield strength and tensile ductility.
Load-aligned elongated grains avoid grain boundaries inclined at approximately 45° to the loading direction and thereby suppress shear failure along weak boundaries.
Reducing the brittle intermetallic fraction prevents premature fracture initiation.
The annealed alloy maintains a fine, coherent precipitate distribution.
The remaining fine γ′ precipitates provide solid-solution and precipitation hardening that raises yield strength.
The aligned grains and reduced intermetallic content promote uniform dislocation glide and strain hardening instead of crack propagation.
A reticulated or fine precipitate structure promotes strain hardening.
The resulting yield strength will be comparable to or greater than the base alloy's ultimate tensile strength.
The optimized treatment increases tensile elongation to failure.
Directional solidification and optimized annealing reduce scatter in tensile properties.
Annealing at 950 °C for 100 h leaves about 9% Heusler phase, coarser γ′ precipitates, lower UTS, lower strain to failure, and greater scatter than annealing at 900 °C for 50 h.
Conventional casting followed by high-temperature annealing produces an equiaxed grain structure.
The proposed route applies only when brittleness is governed by grain-boundary shear and brittle intermetallic formation, rather than intrinsic lattice instability.
Optimal withdrawal speed and annealing parameters vary substantially with composition because phase-transformation and grain-growth kinetics are composition-dependent.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies 900 °C/50 h as the beneficial anneal and 950 °C/100 h as an inferior treatment. Consequently, failure of directionally solidified Set C treated at 950 °C/100 h to improve ductility over Set B does not falsify the proposed role of the optimized 900 °C/50 h treatment; it is compatible with the hypothesis. Moreover, Sets B and C differ in both solidification route and annealing schedule, so that comparison cannot isolate the annealing mechanism.
